questions.explanation: Renewability is about the rate of replacement relative to the rate of use, not about whether the resource is natural or whether it can be reused. Solar radiation arrives continuously and tidal movement reverses on a fixed cycle, so both are replenished faster than they can be exhausted; groundwater is a stock that is recharged by infiltration, which on any human timescale is slower than the rate at which a coastal aquifer is pumped, so treating it as renewable in the same sense is a category error. The renewable and non-renewable distinction is therefore a statement about rates, and the claim that a non-renewable resource cannot be used twice is irrelevant: coal used once is still coal, and a wave used once does not stop being a renewable source.

questions.explanation: A stock has accumulated over a period far longer than any human planning horizon and is drawn down each time it is extracted, so a coal seam shrinks with every tonne removed and cannot be replaced on the timescale of the extraction. The distinction matters because it sets the limit: on a flow the constraint is a rate, and exceeding it depletes the flow, while on a stock the constraint is the total and the only permanent test is what is left in the ground. questions.explanation: The two channels usually cited run in opposite directions but share one origin, the flow of rent from extraction. First, a government living on rent spends it freely and has no need to tax its own citizens, so it builds no broader tax base and lets manufacturing and agriculture be crowded out by an easier revenue source; when the mine depletes or the price falls, that revenue vanishes with nothing underneath it. Second, the export earnings that the rent brings in bid up the currency, which makes every other export uncompetitive and every import cheap, so the non-extractive economy withers. The symptom of falling real revenue alongside a rising cost of living is the signature of the second channel, since a strong currency makes imported food dearer while the rent itself shrinks.

questions.explanation: An enclave economy is one in which a modern sector is geographically and commercially detached from the rest of the economy, and the weakness is that the money it generates does not circulate domestically. Wages are spent, but a large share leaves as profit, imported equipment and debt service; even the wages that stay buy little that a local supplier makes. The result is a small domestic multiplier: the mine is a large export earner and a large employer, but the surrounding economy is barely affected, and both remain hostage to a single world price. The arrangement is not automatically harmful, since it brings foreign exchange and infrastructure, but the leakage is the part that has to be weighed, and the answers offered as alternatives either reverse the direction of the flow or mistake dependence for insulation.

answer.exemplar: A single-crop export has a narrow picking window, so labour is needed in a burst and then not at all, and the employer has an interest in keeping the workforce near the estate for the duration. Company housing tied to the employment, and payment held until the round is finished, mean that a worker who leaves early forfeits both the roof and the wage, so the labour is available but not free to move. The arrangement also standardises the crop: pickers paid by weight take only ripe fruit, which suits a processor and keeps the estate's output uniform. The system is expensive to maintain and politically contentious, and it is exactly the dependency that a minimum wage, worker documentation and independent housing would dissolve.

questions.explanation: Dependency here is produced by timing and residence rather than by force. A plantation crop has one harvest window in the year, so the employer wants pickers present and on site for that window and indifferent for the rest of the year, and the company supplies the housing and pays out at the end of it, which makes leaving early a decision to give up a wage and a roof at once. The same arrangement disciplines the crop, since payment by weight pushes workers towards ripe fruit, which is what a processor needs and what a smallholder selling on a contract does not have to do. The trap is to read the seasonal pattern as evidence of surplus labour instead: the number of pickers needed is set by the harvest window, not by the size of the resident workforce.

questions.explanation: A lender making a seasonal loan needs something it can convert to cash if the borrower defaults, and a registered plot is the usual candidate because it can be sold. answer.exemplar: The controls act at different points in the growth of a pest population and at different speeds, and combining them means the fast measures usually hold the population below the level that damages the crop. Scouting establishes what is actually present, so the spray is applied where and when there is something to spray for, rather than on a calendar across every plot. The predator works continuously but only slowly, and the trap crop concentrates the pest at the edge where it can be removed, so neither would be enough alone and both reduce the area that has to be treated. Because the spray is now a last step reached rarely, the volume falls steeply while the loss does not, and the reason it falls is fewer applications rather than weaker ones. The costs are the scouting labour, the delay before a genuine outbreak is seen, and the need for the predator to be present early enough.

questions.explanation: What makes the combination work is that no single measure is quick enough to be the only one. A predator multiplies too slowly to stop an outbreak on its own, a trap crop removes only the fraction that migrates into it, and neither can tell a manager whether anything is present, so a programme that relies on any of them alone is relying on a lag. Scouting supplies the missing information and converts spraying from a routine into a response, which is where most of the saving comes from, because the last step is then applied to a few plots rather than all of them. Crop loss is not rising because the population is being held below its damaging density continuously, rather than being allowed to build and then knocked back after damage has occurred. The honest costs are the scouting labour, the delay in recognising a real outbreak, and the dependence on the predator arriving in time.
questions.hint: Consider what each control does to the population before it reaches the damaging level.
questions.learningObjective: explain how combining controls reduces sprayed volume without raising losses

questions.explanation: The deposit is a stock, so the industry is drawing down an accumulation rather than tapping a flow, and every tonne extracted reduces what remains while adding nothing back. The income that the state now earns is a conversion of stored natural wealth into current spending, and it is therefore a transfer between the present and the future rather than a return on a renewable yield. For income to continue once the extraction stops, something else has to take the place of the depleted wealth, and the only candidates are other assets, other sectors or higher productivity on the assets already held. This is why mineral booms so often end in a fiscal problem: the revenue was spent as though it were a yield, and the stock it came from is smaller every year.

answer.exemplar: Two effects run in parallel, and both are about the same rent arriving at once. On the fiscal side, a government that can finance itself from oil revenue has no reason to tax its citizens, so it builds no tax administration and gives the non-extractive economy no reason to formalise; when the oil revenue falls, the state has neither reserves nor a collection system, and the adjustment is a fiscal crisis. On the exchange side, the export earnings bid up the currency, which makes every other export uncompetitive and every imported good cheap, so tradable agriculture and manufacturing contract while the country grows dependent on one commodity. A third effect compounds both, since a skilled, mobile workforce is drawn into the extractive sector, raising wages in the modern economy and making the sectors that would have employed it less viable. Depreciation, exchange-rate appreciation and rentier expectations reinforce one another, so the diagnosis is a structure rather than a sequence of unfortunate events.

questions.explanation: The paradox is that the windfall is spent before anyone has built the economy that could replace it. The rent gives the government an alternative to taxation, so public services and infrastructure are paid for out of extraction instead of out of the productive sectors, and the tax administration that a broadening economy would have forced into existence never appears. Meanwhile the currency appreciates on the export inflows, which is a tax on every other export and a subsidy on every import, so the tradable sectors that were the state's only alternative grow less competitive while they are being asked to compete. The labour market adds a third strand, since the extractive sector bids up wages and takes the skilled workers that manufacturing and modern agriculture would have used. Each effect makes the state more dependent on the one source, and the trigger for the reversal is a fall in price or in output, at which point there is no second engine to start.
questions.hint: Follow the rent into the fiscal system and into the exchange rate, in that order.
questions.learningObjective: explain how rent from extraction can damage the non-extractive economy

questions.explanation: A forward linkage is an activity the enterprise undertakes itself that could instead have been bought from outside, because building it keeps the spending and the capability in the domestic economy. answer.exemplar: The station result is a return under conditions the trial controls: the water is there, the nutrients are applied on a schedule someone else pays for, and the season is monitored. On a field those conditions are rented from a household whose income has to be earned from the same field, so each input is judged on whether it can be repaid in a bad year as well as a good one, and an input that doubles the yield in a good year while risking the crop in a dry one may be rejected. Credit adds a second constraint, because the improved seed and the fertiliser must be bought before the harvest and a household without collateral cannot borrow to buy them, which converts a technical gap into a financial one. The remaining constraints are informational, since the trial result was obtained on plots selected for suitability, and structural, since a small holder cannot spread the fixed cost of a new practice over enough hectares. Closing the gap therefore means removing one of these constraints, not telling farmers about another variety.

questions.explanation: A yield gap is a gap in the conditions as much as in the knowledge, and the conditions at a trial station are supplied rather than earned. Water, nutrients and pest control all cost money or labour that a household risks on the same season's income, so a practice is adopted only when it can be repaid even if the season is poor, which is a stricter test than the one a controlled trial measures. Finance deepens the same problem, since the inputs have to be bought before the revenue arrives and a household with no collateral cannot bridge that gap, so the technically best option is unavailable to exactly the households the gap is largest for. Information and scale compound it: trial plots are chosen for suitability, and a small holder has too few hectares to spread the fixed cost of learning or of a new implement. The practical conclusion is that the gap closes where a constraint is removed, whether irrigation, credit, an extension service or a market, rather than where a recommendation is merely circulated.
questions.hint: Consider who bears the cost of a failed season and who owns the benefit of an improved practice.
questions.learningObjective: explain why the gap between potential and achieved yield persists

questions.explanation: The transfer has converted income earned in one economy into income paid out of another, and in doing so it has tied the household to a labour market in a city it does not live in and to a policy environment it does not vote in. A shock there, a factory closure or a change in immigration rules, removes nearly half the household's income at once, and no decision taken in the village can bring it back. The change is not simply that income has risen, because the terms on which it is now earned are outside the household's control, and the transfer is usually worth more than the alternative local wage for the same work, which is why it is not simply reversed. The gains are real and the spending they fund often becomes permanent, so the question is about the shape of the risk rather than whether the arrangement is rational.

answer.exemplar: A lease is a claim on this season's crop, and a title is a claim on the asset itself, and the two support different decisions. A soil fertility programme, a terrace, a drainage ditch or a planting that takes three seasons to pay back will not be made on a lease that might not be renewed, because the cost is certain and immediate while the benefit accrues to whoever is farming the plot next. Once the operator holds the asset, the same investment becomes sound, and there is also a reason to maintain rather than extract, since the value of the plot is itself part of what the household owns. The reform does not create water, credit or markets, and it does not raise yields on its own, so it is easy to overstate: what it changes is the time horizon over which a decision pays, which is enough to move the input rate considerably when the constraint on investment is tenure rather than money.

questions.explanation: The decision at issue is a comparison between an immediate cost and a distant benefit, and tenure decides how far ahead a household must be willing to look. On a yearly lease the household is not the residual claimant, so it captures only one season of the return on a change that takes three or five to pay back, and the rational response is to extract rather than invest; the consequence is a plot that is farmed harder each year and deteriorates, with soil structure and fertility falling as the tenancy lengthens. A registered title makes the household the residual claimant, so the same investment is sound, and it also gives a reason to maintain the asset since the plot's value is part of what is owned. The reform should not be oversold, since it supplies no water, no credit and no market, and where the binding constraint is a lack of capital the tenure change alone will move little; its effect is largest where insecurity was the reason capital was not applied.
questions.hint: Consider the length of the payback period on the improvements a farm can make.
questions.learningObjective: explain how tenure security alters the horizon of farm investment

The trap is treating efficiency as a share of the water required rather than of the water applied, which gives a different and much larger volume.

answer.exemplar: A falling share of work on farms, a falling number of farms and a rising average income are exactly what a successful agriculture looks like, and they are also exactly what a process of people leaving farming looks like, so the figures are consistent with at least two quite different stories. The counts are the place to start, and they are more revealing than the report suggests: two thirds of the farms at a half more income each is exactly the total, so farm income as a whole has not risen at all while the average per farm has gone up by half. That is the arithmetic of concentration, with fewer holdings each producing more, and it is equally the arithmetic of loss, with the holdings that vanished having taken their income with them. Nothing in the figures reports what happened to the two fifths of the workforce that left farm work: if they are in local non-farm employment the claim may hold, and if they are unemployed or have migrated, the district's rural economy has lost the labour on which the surviving farms depended. A report of this kind should report the destination of the released workers, because that is the figure that decides between the two readings.

questions.explanation: The claim is a claim about structure, and every figure given is a figure about size, so nothing in them rules out the possibility that the district has simply lost people. The counts are the strongest evidence against the claim, and they are more revealing than the report suggests: two thirds as many farms at a half more income each multiplies out to exactly the same total, so farm income as a whole has not risen by so much as a single unit while the reported average has gone up by half. That is the arithmetic of concentration rather than of growth, and it is equally the arithmetic of loss, since the holdings that disappeared took their share of income with them. The workforce figure sharpens the problem, because a fall of two fifths in farm work is presented as productivity when it is equally consistent with those workers having no local employment at all. Diversification would have to be shown by where that labour went and by the range of activities now present, none of which appears in the figures quoted.
questions.hint: Work out what has happened to the people who left farm work, and count the people as well as the holdings.

questions.explanation: Renewability is a rate question, and here the recharge rate is below the abstraction rate, so on any timescale a planner actually works to the aquifer is being drawn down. The classification follows from the balance rather than from what the water is: an aquifer does not become a non-renewable resource because it is old or because it is deep, it becomes one when recharge cannot replace what is removed. The consequence is that the resource behaves like a stock, so the sustainable abstraction is the recharge figure and pumping above it is a withdrawal against capital, with the cost appearing later as a deeper bore, a poorer yield, or saline intrusion where seawater is drawn in. The distractors each misattribute the classification to a property that does not bear on it.

questions.explanation: The land is stated to be fixed while the town's demand is growing, so the binding constraint is output per hectare, and the comparison has to be made on that basis rather than on labour, on distance or on the area planted. Irrigated vegetables yield far more food per hectare than grain, and grain yields far more than hand-tool millet, so the ranking follows the energy and water each system puts into the hectare. The systems also differ in where their inputs come from, since imported grain and pumped water are costs paid elsewhere, and that belongs in the comparison as well. The option counting hectares is measuring the input that is fixed rather than the one that is scarce, and the option counting workers answers an employment question that the stem does not pose.
questions.hint: Identify the scarce input in the district, and rank the systems on the use of that input.

questions.explanation: The business counts fall steadily as the connection is delayed, from 42 to 31 to 18 to 9, so that column behaves as an association would. The income changes do not: 12, 20, 27 and 19 rise and then fall, so that column is not monotone in the connection date and cannot be read the same way. This is the ordinary position with a four-row table of real districts, since other differences between the districts, in starting income, in rainfall, in distance to a market, move both outcomes at once, and nothing in the table holds them constant. The honest reading is therefore that one column is consistent with an effect and the other is not, and that establishing a cause would need either a longer series or a design that fixes the other differences. Refusing to compare four districts at all is a different mistake, and is not warranted by the sample size.
questions.hint: Check each of the two outcome columns against the connection date separately.

questions.explanation: The ceiling is the stated share of the stated verified value, so 0.40 times 40,000 dollars is 16,000, and the rule holds for every member on the same valuation basis. Leaving that margin is deliberate: land values fall, valuations are disputed, sale takes time and costs, and a lender who advanced the full verified value would be exposed the moment any of those went against it. The advance rate is therefore the institution's own statement of how much of the security it is prepared to rely on, and it is set the same way for everyone so that a member's ceiling is a fact about the collateral rather than a judgement about the borrower. The options using 24,000 or 40,000 ignore the rule, and the option repeating 16,000 offers a rationale about the member rather than about the security.
questions.hint: Apply the stated share to the stated verified value, and ask what makes the rule a rule.

questions.explanation: A falling water table is the recharge side of a rainfall deficit, since a well has to be deepened as the saturated zone retreats from the surface and the cost of every additional metre rises. The community's response is the classic pastoral adaptation, moving or destocking, and the families that have sold their animals and settled are the ones who have exited the system rather than adjusted to it. That exit is itself the evidence, because it is expensive: animals are the household's capital and its insurance in the same asset, so selling them is a decision taken when the trajectory looks permanent rather than a reaction to one bad season. The reading depends on the trend rather than on a single dry year, and the options that turn on rising water, on a policy decision or on water chemistry do not fit a decade-long deepening.
questions.hint: Ask why it takes progressively deeper holes to reach water that used to be near the surface.
questions.learningObjective: read a falling water table as a rainfall deficit in pastoral systems

options.misconception: offers a salinity story for a depth story, which is a different failure mode

questions.explanation: The two remittance figures measure different things and one village separates them. Village C has the largest remittance share of income at 61 per cent, yet only 12 per cent of its households receive anything, so a small number of families carry a very large part of the village's income. C is also losing households. That combination is the concentration risk: the village is exposed to the labour market of the cities its few recipients work in, and a shock there reaches a group too small to replace from within the village economy. The other villages are the mirror image in part, with A and B combining wider receipt with growth. The claim that dependence rises with headcount is contradicted by A and B, and the claim that remittances cause the losses is contradicted by two villages that receive them and grow.
questions.hint: Look for a village whose income dependence and its reach among households point in different directions.

questions.explanation: The sequence starts with the inflows themselves, since nothing else is possible without them. The exchange rate responds almost immediately, because export earnings have to be exchanged and that demand for the domestic currency bids it up, and the appreciation lands on the tradable sector as a tax, making every other export less competitive at exactly the moment there is new money to import with. The fiscal response comes in parallel but its consequences come later: revenue spent without a domestic tax base being built means the tradable sectors are being crowded out at the same time as they are being penalised by the currency, and their contraction is the joint result. The reversal comes last, when the price or the output falls and the state discovers it has neither reserves nor a second industry to fall back on, which is the stage the deficit belongs to.
questions.hint: The currency effect follows directly from the inflows, and the contraction follows from what the state did with the revenue.
